claim: De novo mutations in the RNA helicase, DDX3X, are one of the leading causes of ID in females and underlie DDX3X syndrome.
source: De novo mutations in the RNA helicase, DDX3X, are one of the leading causes of ID in females and underlie DDX3X syndrome (Beal et al., 2019; Lennox et al., 2020; Scala et al., 2019; Snijders Blok et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature establishing DDX3X mutations as a leading cause of intellectual disability.

claim: DDX3X is X-linked, which likely explains the preponderance of female cases.
source: DDX3X is X-linked, which likely explains the preponderance of female cases; although an increasing number of de novo and inherited DDX3X mutations are found in males (Kellaris et al., 2018; Nicola et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations and established knowledge that X-linked genes affect females more frequently due to X-inactivation patterns.

claim: Individuals with DDX3X syndrome commonly present with muscle tone and gait abnormalities, language deficits, abnormal brain MRIs (particularly white matter loss and corpus callosum defects), and many are diagnosed with ASD.
source: While DDX3X syndrome is characterized by ID, these individuals also commonly present with muscle tone and gait abnormalities, language deficits, abnormal brain MRIs (particularly white matter loss and corpus callosum defects), and many are diagnosed with ASD (Johnson-Kerner et al., 1993; Lennox et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies describing phenotypes of DDX3X syndrome patients.

claim: DDX3X mutations have been identified in ASD cohorts, and DDX3X is considered a high-confidence Autism gene.
source: Indeed, DDX3X mutations have been identified in ASD cohorts, and DDX3X is considered a high-confidence Autism gene (Iossifov et al., 2014; Ruzzo et al., 2019; Takata et al., 2018; Yuen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies identifying DDX3X mutations in autism cohorts.

claim: DDX3X mutations have been linked to cancer progression, including medulloblastoma.
source: DDX3X mutations have also been linked to cancer progression, including medulloblastoma (Jones, 2012; Pugh, 2012; Robinson et al., 2012), many of which overlap with ID-associated mutations.
evidence: Supported by citations to cancer genomics studies.

claim: DDX3X has conserved functions in cell cycle progression.
source: This oncogenic role is consistent with conserved functions of DDX3X in cell cycle progression (Chen et al., 2016a; Kotov et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014; Zhang and Li, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating DDX3X's role in cell cycle.

claim: Cell cycle duration is strongly implicated in cortical development.
source: Notably, cell cycle duration is also strongly implicated in cortical development (Arai et al., 2011; Lange et al., 2009; Pilaz et al., 2016; Pilaz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental neuroscience studies.

claim: Over 100 de novo mutations have been identified in DDX3X syndrome, equally composed of nonsense/frameshift and missense mutations.
source: Remarkably, over 100 de novo mutations have been identified in DDX3X syndrome, equally composed of nonsense/frameshift and missense (Johnson-Kerner et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical genetics literature.

claim: In female mice, Ddx3x germline haploinsufficiency impairs postnatal brain architecture and causes behavioral deficits phenocopying aspects of human DDX3X syndrome.
source: Consistent with this, in female mice, Ddx3x germline haploinsufficiency impairs postnatal brain architecture and causes behavioral deficits phenocopying aspects of human DDX3X syndrome (Boitnott et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a mouse model study.

claim: Acute Ddx3x depletion in a subset of cells perturbed progenitor and neuron number.
source: In addition, using transient CRISPR approaches we previously showed that acute Ddx3x depletion in a subset of cells perturbed progenitor and neuron number (Lennox et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: DDX3X is a cytoplasmic RNA helicase that promotes translation of mRNAs with highly structured 5′ UTRs.
source: DDX3X is a cytoplasmic RNA helicase that promotes translation of mRNAs with highly structured 5′ UTRs (Calviello et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to molecular biology studies characterizing DDX3X function.

claim: DDX3X translational targets have been characterized in immortalized cells but not in the developing brain in vivo.
source: Although DDX3X translational targets have been characterized in immortalized cells (Calviello et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2016), they have not been identified in the developing brain in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations and statement of gap in knowledge.

claim: Translational control is essential for corticogenesis.
source: Further, while translational control is essential for corticogenesis (Blair et al., 2017; Hoye and Silver, 2021; Kraushar et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014; Zahr et al., 2018), there is limited genome-wide assessment of translation in the developing cortex, which restricts our understanding of this important layer of post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on translational control in brain development.

claim: Ddx3x mRNA levels were ~30% reduced in cHet females, ~40% reduced in cKO males and ~70% reduced in cKO females relative to their respective sex-matched controls at E11.5.
source: At E11.5, Ddx3x mRNA levels were ~30% reduced in cHet females,~40% reduced in cKO males and ~70% reduced in cKO females relative to their respective sex-matched controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Control females expressed ~25% higher levels of Ddx3x than control males.
source: Notably, control females expressed ~25% higher levels of Ddx3x than control males (Figure 1G), which was similarly evident in the quantification of smFISH data.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G and smFISH quantification.

claim: The significant difference in Ddx3x levels between control females and males suggests Ddx3x partially escapes X chromosome inactivation (XCI) in the embryonic cortex.
source: The significant difference in Ddx3x levels between control females and males is consistent with previous findings in mice and humans (Tukiainen, 2017; Wu et al., 2014) and suggests Ddx3x partially escapes X chromosome inactivation (XCI) in the embryonic cortex.
evidence: Inferred from observed expression differences and supported by citations to XCI studies.

claim: Homozygous loss of Ddx3x from neural progenitors and their progeny led to profound microcephaly in cKO females at postnatal day 0 (P0).
source: Strikingly, homozygous loss of Ddx3x from neural progenitors and their progeny led to profound microcephaly in cKO females at postnatal day 0 (P0) (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by cortical area measurements shown in Figure 1H, I.

claim: The decrease in cortical area in cKO females began at E14.5, and by P0 was reduced by 50%.
source: The decrease in cortical area began at E14.5, and by P0 was reduced by 50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by temporal quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant reduction in cortical area was observed in cHet females or cKO males.
source: In contrast, no significant reduction in cortical area was observed in cHet females or cKO males (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by cortical area measurements shown in Figure 1H, I.

claim: Approximately 5% of cells in cKO females were CC3+ at E12.5 and ~15% were CC3+ at E14.5.
source: We observed ~5% of cells in cKO females were CC3+ at E12.5 and ~15% were CC3+ at E14.5 (Figure 1J and K; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis quantification shown in Figure 1J, K and supplementary figures.

claim: Apoptotic cells in cKO females were both Tuj1+ and Tuj1-, suggesting complete Ddx3x loss causes death of both progenitors and newborn neurons.
source: Apoptotic cells were both Tuj1+ and Tuj1-, suggesting complete Ddx3x loss causes death of both progenitors and newborn neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Inferred from immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CC3+ cells were not detected at either E12.5 or E14.5 in cHet females and cKO males.
source: In contrast, and consistent with the absence of microcephaly in cHet females and cKO males, CC3 + cells were not detected at either E12.5 or E14.5 in these genotypes (Figure 1J; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis quantification shown in Figure 1J and supplementary figures.

claim: Microcephaly and apoptosis were not observed in Nex-Cre, cKO females across cortical development.
source: Unlike Emx1-Cre cKO females, we did not observe microcephaly or apoptosis in Nex-Cre, cKO females across cortical development (E13.5, E15.5, E17.5 (not shown) and P0; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: Apoptosis of newborn neurons in the Emx1-Cre model is due to defects in neural precursors.
source: This suggests that apoptosis of newborn neurons in the Emx1-Cre model is due to defects in neural precursors.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Emx1-Cre and Nex-Cre models.

claim: In E11.5 Ddx3x cKO male cortices, Ddx3y mRNA levels were significantly elevated 1.4 fold on average.
source: In E11.5 Ddx3x cKO male cortices, Ddx3y mRNA levels were significantly elevated 1.4 fold on average (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a transcriptional adaptation of Ddx3y in response to reduced Ddx3x in the embryonic cortex.
source: This suggests there is a transcriptional adaptation of Ddx3y in response to reduced Ddx3x in the embryonic cortex, consistent with findings in Ddx3x cKO hindbrains (Patmore et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from observed Ddx3y upregulation and supported by citation to similar findings in hindbrain.

claim: Ddx3y sgRNA resulted in an average 53% reduction in Ddx3y mRNA levels with no effect upon Ddx3x mRNA expression.
source: Using FACS to isolate GFP+ cells from E17.5 brains, we quantified an average 53% reduction in Ddx3y mRNA levels following Ddx3y CRISPR-based depletion; there was no effect upon Ddx3x mRNA expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ddx3y knockdown led to the accumulation of GFP+ cells in the VZ, with few GFP+ cells in the CP.
source: Conversely, Ddx3y knockdown led to the accumulation of GFP+ cells in the VZ, with few GFP+ cells in the CP (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: Supported by cell distribution data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: Ddx3y depletion led to significantly more progenitors and fewer neurons, as compared to control.
source: Quantification of GFP+Sox2+ progenitors and GFP+Neurod2+ neurons showed that Ddx3y depletion led to significantly more progenitors and fewer neurons, as compared to control (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: Ddx3y depletion phenocopies acute Ddx3x knockdown by IUE in the embryonic brain.
source: Importantly, these findings phenocopy acute Ddx3x knockdown by IUE in the embryonic brain (Lennox et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Ddx3x and Ddx3y have similar requirements for neurogenesis.
source: This demonstrates that Ddx3x and Ddx3y have similar requirements for neurogenesis, suggesting that Ddx3y partially compensates for Ddx3x in cKO males.
evidence: Inferred from phenocopy experiments showing similar effects of Ddx3x and Ddx3y depletion.

claim: Ddx3y partially compensates for Ddx3x in cKO males.
source: This demonstrates that Ddx3x and Ddx3y have similar requirements for neurogenesis, suggesting that Ddx3y partially compensates for Ddx3x in cKO males.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cKO males have milder phenotypes than cKO females and Ddx3y depletion phenocopies Ddx3x loss.

claim: The number of RGCs and mature IPs was significantly increased in Ddx3x depleted brains at E14.5.
source: However, by E14.5, the number of RGCs and mature IPs was significantly increased in Ddx3x depleted brains (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: There was a concomitant trend towards fewer Tbr2-Sox2- cells following Ddx3x depletion at both E13.5 and E14.5, suggesting potentially fewer neurons.
source: Moreover, there was a concomitant trend towards fewer Tbr2-Sox2- cells following Ddx3x depletion at both E13.5 and E14.5, suggesting potentially fewer neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: The number of Tbr1 (Layer VI) and Ctip2 (Layer V) neurons was significantly reduced in Ddx3x depleted mice at P0.
source: The number of Tbr1 (Layer VI) and Ctip2 (Layer V) neurons was significantly reduced in Ddx3x depleted mice, and there was a trend towards reduced Lhx2 (Layer II/III) (P=0.078) (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: Laminar distribution was unaffected in Ddx3x depleted mice, suggesting that Ddx3x is largely dispensable for neuronal migration.
source: However, laminar distribution was unaffected, suggesting that Ddx3x is largely dispensable for neuronal migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Supported by distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: At E14.5, there were significantly more EdU+Ki67+ cells in Ddx3x depleted brains relative to control.
source: At E14.5, there were significantly more EdU+Ki67+ cells in Ddx3x depleted brains relative to control (Figure 4A–C), indicating that Ddx3x is required for progenitor cell cycle exit.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle exit quantification shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: There were significantly more EdU+Sox2+ cells in Ddx3x depleted brains compared to control, indicating reduced cell cycle exit of RGCs.
source: We measured significantly more EdU+Sox2+ cells in Ddx3x depleted brains compared to control, indicating reduced cell cycle exit of RGCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was a significant concomitant decrease in EdU+Sox2-Tbr2- cells (putative neurons) in Ddx3x depleted brains relative to control.
source: Moreover, there was a significant concomitant decrease in EdU+Sox2-Tbr2- cells (putative neurons) in Ddx3x depleted brains relative to control (Figure 4E), suggesting that Ddx3x depletion perturbs generation of neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ddx3x depleted brains exhibited a significantly longer cell cycle (Tc) than control, nearly 1.5-fold longer (average 17 hr in ctrl vs 25 hr in cHet F/cKO M).
source: Strikingly, the Ddx3x depleted brains exhibited a significantly longer cell cycle (Tc) than control, nearly 1.5-fold longer (average 17 hr in ctrl vs 25 hr in cHet F/cKO M) (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle duration measurements shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Ddx3x depletion did not specifically impair S phase duration as Ts/Tc was not significantly different.
source: However, Ddx3x depletion did not specifically impair S phase duration as Ts/Tc was not significantly different (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by S phase quantification shown in Figure 4I.

claim: There was no significant difference in the percentage of phospho-histone3 (PH3)+Sox2+ cells between controls and Ddx3x depleted brains, indicating that G2/M length of RGCs is not specifically affected.
source: Further, there was no significant difference in the percentage of phospho-histone3 (PH3)+Sox2+ cells between controls and Ddx3x depleted brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D) indicating that G2/M length of RGCs is not specifically affected.
evidence: Supported by PH3 quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Ddx3x depleted cells underwent significantly fewer re-divisions relative to controls.
source: Consistent with a prolonged cell cycle duration, Ddx3x depleted cells underwent significantly fewer re-divisions relative to controls (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: Ddx3x depleted progenitors underwent significantly more proliferative (P,P) divisions and significantly fewer symmetric neurogenic (N,N) divisions relative to controls.
source: Ddx3x depleted progenitors underwent significantly more proliferative (P,P) divisions and significantly fewer symmetric neurogenic (N,N) divisions relative to controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by cell fate quantification from live imaging shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Asymmetric neurogenic (N,P) divisions were unchanged in Ddx3x depleted progenitors.
source: Asymmetric neurogenic (N,P) divisions were unchanged.
evidence: Stated in the context of cell fate analysis.

claim: At E11.5, RGC-, IP-, and deep layer neuron-enriched transcripts all had significantly higher TE than the average transcript expressed at this stage.
source: To our surprise we found that at E11.5, RGC-, IP-, and deep layer neuron-enriched transcripts all had significantly higher TE than the average transcript expressed at this stage (other genes), consistent with translational upregulation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by translation efficiency analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a notable divergence between deep (positive TE) and superficial (negative TE) layer neuron transcripts at E11.5.
source: Moreover, there was a notable divergence between deep (positive TE) and superficial (negative TE) layer neuron transcripts (Figure 6B), suggesting superficial layer neuron transcripts are translationally repressed.
evidence: Supported by translation efficiency analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Early progenitors use translational priming to direct cell fate in addition to transcriptional priming.
source: This suggests that in addition to transcriptional priming, early progenitors also use translational priming to direct cell fate.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transcripts for future cell types show differential translation efficiency.

claim: ORFquant analysis revealed ~14,000 annotated ORFs and ~2500 uORFs in cortical progenitors.
source: This revealed ~14,000 annotated ORFs and ~2500 uORFs, including a prominent uORF in the lissencephaly gene, Pafah1b1 or Lis1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ORFquant analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ORFquant analysis identified ~1200 ORFs in non-coding RNAs, including a novel ORF in the Rab26os lncRNA.
source: We also identified ~1200 ORFs in non-coding RNAs, including a novel ORF in the Rab26os lncRNA (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Supported by ORFquant analysis shown in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claim: 147 targets had differential TE (p-adjusted <0.05) in Ddx3x cKO data.
source: We then turned to our Ddx3x cKO data to discover DDX3X-dependent translation targets and identified 147 targets that had differential TE (p-adjusted <0.05) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by differential translation efficiency analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Virtually all DDX3X translation targets (144 of 147) had a lower TE in cKO mice, consistent with DDX3X promoting translation.
source: Virtually all targets (144 of 147) had a lower TE in cKO mice, consistent with DDX3X promoting translation.
evidence: Supported by differential translation efficiency analysis.

claim: Rcor2 and Topbp1 mRNA were significantly enriched in the monosome fraction of cKO females and males relative to controls at E11.5.
source: We observed that Rcor2 and Topbp1 mRNA were signficantly enriched in the monosome fraction of cKO females and males relative to controls, while the HMW polysome fraction was unaltered (Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by polysome fractionation data shown in Figure 6J and supplementary figures.

claim: Both Rcor2 and Setd3 were significantly enriched in the monosome fraction and significantly depleted from the polysome fraction for cHet females/cKO males as compared to controls at E14.5.
source: Both Rcor2 and Setd3 were significantly enriched in the monosome fraction and significantly depleted from the polysome fraction for cHet females/cKO males as compared to controls (Figure 6K, L), consistent with their decreased TE at E11.5.
evidence: Supported by polysome fractionation data shown in Figure 6K, L.

claim: Topbp1 was significantly depleted from the polysome fraction, but unchanged in the monosome fraction in cHet females/cKO males relative to controls at E14.5.
source: Topbp1 was significantly depleted from the polysome fraction, but unchanged in the monosome fraction in cHet females/cKO males relative to controls (Figure 6M).
evidence: Supported by polysome fractionation data shown in Figure 6M.

claim: Rcor2, Setd3, and Topbp1 were significantly upregulated in the input RNA at E14.5 as compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, Rcor2, Setd3, and Topbp1 were also significantly upregulated in the input RNA at E14.5 (Figure 6I) as compared to controls, even though their RNA levels were not significantly changed at E11.5.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: GFP-hDDX3X specifically binds to Rcor2, Setd3, and Topbp1 transcripts.
source: RT-PCR for Rcor2, Setd3, and Topbp1, revealed specific binding to these transcripts by GFP-hDDX3X, but not in untransfected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: RCOR2 is critical for neural proliferation.
source: RCOR2 is critical for neural proliferation (Monaghan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016), and Topbp1 deletion in neural progenitors results in DNA damage and apoptosis (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing RCOR2 and Topbp1 function.

claim: Topbp1 deletion in neural progenitors results in DNA damage and apoptosis.
source: RCOR2 is critical for neural proliferation (Monaghan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016), and Topbp1 deletion in neural progenitors results in DNA damage and apoptosis (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to study characterizing Topbp1 function.

claim: Setd3 knockdown significantly altered the distribution of GFP+ cells, with significantly more cells in the VZ and fewer cells in the CP.
source: Setd3 knockdown significantly altered the distribution of GFP + cells, with significantly more cells in the VZ and fewer cells in the CP (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: Supported by cell distribution data shown in Figure 7B, C.

claim: Setd3 knockdown resulted in more Sox2+ RGCs and fewer Neurod2+ neurons.
source: Moreover, Setd3 knockdown resulted in more Sox2+ RGCs and fewer Neurod2+ neurons (Figure 7D, E), phenocopying Ddx3x LoF.
evidence: Supported by cell type quantification shown in Figure 7D, E.

claim: Setd3 knockdown phenocopies Ddx3x LoF.
source: Moreover, Setd3 knockdown resulted in more Sox2+ RGCs and fewer Neurod2+ neurons (Figure 7D, E), phenocopying Ddx3x LoF.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of phenotypes between Setd3 knockdown and Ddx3x loss.

claim: DDX3X controls translation of a repertoire of genes which are collectively critical in neural progenitors for neurogenesis.
source: Taken together these data show that DDX3X controls translation of a repertoire of genes which are collectively critical in neural progenitors for neurogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the identification of multiple DDX3X-dependent translation targets with known roles in neurogenesis.

claim: Dysregulated progenitor cell cycle dynamics and translation are pathogenic mechanisms in DDX3X syndrome.
source: Our study reveals invaluable new insights into the etiology of DDX3X syndrome, implicating dysregulated progenitor cell cycle dynamics and translation as pathogenic mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings of the study showing cell cycle and translational defects.

claim: The developing brain is sensitive to Ddx3x dosage; complete Ddx3x loss from neural progenitors causes microcephaly in females, whereas hemizygous males and heterozygous females show reduced neurogenesis without marked microcephaly.
source: First, we show brain development is sensitive to Ddx3x dosage; complete Ddx3x loss from neural progenitors causes microcephaly in females, whereas hemizygous males and heterozygous females show reduced neurogenesis without marked microcephaly.
evidence: Supported by the phenotypic analysis of different genotypes showing dose-dependent effects.

claim: Ddx3x loss is sexually dimorphic, as its paralog, Ddx3y, compensates for Ddx3x in the developing male neocortex.
source: In addition, Ddx3x loss is sexually dimorphic, as its paralog, Ddx3y, compensates for Ddx3x in the developing male neocortex.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing Ddx3y upregulation in males and phenocopy of Ddx3x loss upon Ddx3y depletion.

claim: Ddx3x is expressed in the developing cortex.
source: Representative sections of smFISH for Ddx3x in control, cHet female, and cKO male and female E12.5 cortices.
evidence: Shown by smFISH imaging in Figure 1C demonstrating Ddx3x mRNA presence in cortical tissue.

claim: The Emx1-Cre driver is active in neural progenitors beginning at E9.5.
source: This strategy removes Ddx3x from neural progenitors beginning at E9.5, as well as their progeny.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Emx1-Cre expression pattern.

claim: The Nex-Cre driver is active in post-mitotic excitatory neurons beginning at E12.5.
source: To understand how Ddx3x loss impacts neuronal survival, we used Neurod6-Cre (herein referred to by alias, Nex-Cre), which is active in post-mitotic excitatory neurons beginning at E12.5, to generate Nex-Cre, cKO females (Nex-Cre;Ddx3xlox/lox) (Goebbels et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Nex-Cre expression pattern and supported by citation.

claim: Ddx3y can compensate for Ddx3x at the translational level in immortalized cells.
source: Notably, males have a Ddx3x paralog, Ddx3y, on the Y chromosome which can compensate for Ddx3x at the translational level in immortalized cells (Venkataramanan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to study demonstrating functional redundancy.

claim: Ddx3y can compensate for Ddx3x in the hindbrain.
source: Likewise, in both the hindbrain and hematopoietic system, Ddx3y can also compensate for loss of Ddx3x in vivo (Patmore et al., 2020; Szappanos et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in other tissues.

claim: Ddx3y can compensate for Ddx3x in the hematopoietic system.
source: Likewise, in both the hindbrain and hematopoietic system, Ddx3y can also compensate for loss of Ddx3x in vivo (Patmore et al., 2020; Szappanos et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in other tissues.

claim: DDX3Y normalizes total DDX3 levels between males and females.
source: Because Ddx3x partially escapes XCI in females (Figure 1), we hypothesize that DDX3Y normalizes total DDX3 levels between males and females; this may explain why cHet females and cKO males have comparable phenotypes.
evidence: Hypothesized based on observed expression patterns and phenotypic similarities.

claim: Neural cells of the developing cortex are sensitive to Ddx3x knockout, as loss of one versus two copies causes vastly different corticogenesis phenotypes.
source: In addition to being sexually dimorphic, we discover that neural cells of the developing cortex are sensitive to Ddx3x knockout, as loss of one versus two copies causes vastly different corticogenesis phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes across different genotypes.

claim: DDX3X controls the function of neural progenitors and generation of excitatory neurons throughout cortical development through two key mechanisms: increasing progenitor cell cycle duration and controlling the balance of proliferative versus neurogenic divisions.
source: We show that DDX3X controls the function of neural progenitors and generation of excitatory neurons throughout cortical development through two key mechanisms. First, Ddx3x depletion increases progenitor cell cycle duration by 1.4-fold... Second, Ddx3x controls the balance of proliferative versus neurogenic divisions, resulting in reduced generation of neurons.
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis and live imaging data.

claim: If the increase in cell cycle duration in Ddx3x depleted progenitors were sustained over the course of neurogenesis, it would result in overall fewer progenitor divisions, and ultimately fewer neurons.
source: Additionally, Ddx3x depleted progenitors in vitro underwent fewer re-divisions in a 24-hr period; if this increase in cell cycle duration were sustained over the course of neurogenesis, we predict it would result in overall fewer progenitor divisions, and ultimately fewer neurons (Takahashi et al., 1995).
evidence: Predicted based on observed cell cycle changes and supported by citation to relevant literature.

claim: DDX3X functions in progenitors to direct neural fates of daughter progeny.
source: This is particularly fascinating as it demonstrates that DDX3X functions in progenitors to direct neural fates of daughter progeny.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging data showing altered division types.

claim: RGCs may be especially sensitive to loss of DDX3X, which is consistent with higher Ddx3x expression in RGCs relative to IPs.
source: Ddx3x depletion had a particularly potent impact on RGCs, relative to IPs, suggesting that RGCs may be especially sensitive to loss of DDX3X, which is consistent with higher Ddx3x expression in RGCs relative to IPs (Telley et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from observed phenotypes and supported by citation to expression data.

claim: Germline Ddx3x haploinsufficient females have reduced Ctip2+ (layer V) neurons in the somatosensory cortex at P3, which persists into adulthood.
source: Consistent with our cHet phenotypes, these females were not grossly microcephalic, but did have reduced Ctip2+ (layer V) neurons in the somatosensory cortex at P3, which persisted into adulthood.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from another study.

claim: Germline Ddx3x haploinsufficient mice have overall gross delay, defects in motor coordination, and sensory behavioral abnormalities.
source: These germline mice also have overall gross delay, defects in motor coordination, and sensory behavioral abnormalities.
evidence: Supported by reference to findings from another study.

claim: Ddx3x is largely dispensable in newborn neurons for their migration and survival.
source: Using a Nex-Cre cKO mouse model, we found that Ddx3x is largely dispensable in newborn neurons for their migration and survival, indicating that observed neuronal loss largely arises from impairments in neural progenitors.
evidence: Supported by Nex-Cre model data showing no microcephaly or apoptosis.

claim: Ddx3x controls neurite outgrowth.
source: However, Ddx3x does control neurite outgrowth (Chen et al., 2016b) and is a component of neuronal transport granules (Elvira et al., 2006; Kanai et al., 2004), suggesting it could function in mature neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing DDX3X function in neurons.

claim: Ddx3x is a component of neuronal transport granules.
source: However, Ddx3x does control neurite outgrowth (Chen et al., 2016b) and is a component of neuronal transport granules (Elvira et al., 2006; Kanai et al., 2004), suggesting it could function in mature neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing DDX3X localization.

claim: 50% of DDX3X syndrome individuals present with white matter loss.
source: DDX3X likely functions in other CNS cell types, as well, as 50% of DDX3X syndrome individuals present with white matter loss (Lennox et al., 2020), which could arise from impaired gliogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical characterization study.

claim: Ddx3x depletion alters oligodendrocyte gene expression.
source: Indeed, Perturb-seq of 30 ASD-risk genes found that Ddx3x depletion alters oligodendrocyte gene expression (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perturb-seq study.

claim: DDX3X regulates innate immunity.
source: Moreover, DDX3X also regulates innate immunity (Szappanos et al., 2018), raising the intriguing idea that Ddx3x could function in microglia to influence cortical development.
evidence: Supported by citation to immunology study.

claim: There is limited genome-wide assessment of translation in the developing cortex.
source: In the neurodevelopment field there is a wealth of transcriptomic data, but far less translation/proteomic data for embryonic mouse cortex.
evidence: Based on assessment of available literature in the field.

claim: This is one of the first reports to assess wildtype translation using Ribo-seq at the onset of neurogenesis.
source: To our knowledge, this is one of the first reports to assess wildtype translation using Ribo-seq at the onset of neurogenesis, with exception of a recent pre-print which examined later stages of development (Harnett et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on assessment of available literature and supported by citation.

claim: Transcripts important for deep and superficial layer neuronal fates are expressed in RGCs.
source: scRNAseq studies have revealed that transcripts important for deep and superficial layer neuronal fates are expressed in RGCs Telley et al., 2019; however, it's generally thought that these are translationally repressed until neurons are born.
evidence: Supported by citation to scRNAseq study and established understanding in the field.

claim: The low number of DDX3X translation targets is on-par with translational studies of DDX3X in immortalized cells and reinforces that DDX3X is not a general translation factor.
source: The low number of DDX3X translation targets is on-par with translational studies of DDX3X in immortalized cells and reinforces that DDX3X is not a general translation factor (Calviello et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous DDX3X translational study and comparison of findings.

claim: SETD3 is a histidine methyltransferase, which may modify histone H3, as well as actin H73.
source: SETD3 is a histidine methyltransferase, which may modify histone H3, as well as actin H73 (Witecka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to biochemical characterization study.

claim: Setd3 is implicated in cancer progression and cell cycle control, as well as cytoskeletal integrity.
source: Consistent with this, Setd3 is implicated in cancer progression and cell cycle control, as well as cytoskeletal integrity (Witecka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: Reduced TE of DDX3X-dependent targets may lead to a feedback mechanism whereby these mRNAs are transcriptionally upregulated over time.
source: This could be explained by developmental differences in DD3X levels. Alternatively, it could suggest that reduced TE of DDX3X-dependent targets leads to a feedback mechanism whereby these mRNAs are transcriptionally upregulated over time.
evidence: Speculated based on observed changes in RNA levels over developmental time.

claim: There is a strong association between mutations in translation regulators and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Our work further substantiates the importance of post-transcriptional RNA regulation in cortical development and disease. There is a strong association between mutations in translation regulators and neurodevelopmental disorders (Chen et al., 2019; Hoye and Silver, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles on translational control in neurodevelopment.

claim: Half of DDX3X mutations are missense, with a subset showing more clinically severe outcomes relative to those carrying nonsense mutations.
source: Half of DDX3X mutations are missense, with a subset showing more clinically severe outcomes relative to those carrying nonsense mutations (Lennox et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical characterization study.

claim: DDX3X missense mutations might differentially impair translation of DDX3X targets.
source: Interestingly, DDX3X missense mutations might differentially impair translation of DDX3X targets (Calviello et al., 2021; Lennox et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies examining effects of different mutation types.

claim: Diverse DDX3X mutations may result in divergent molecular and cellular pathologies.
source: Thus, diverse DDX3X mutations may result in divergent molecular and cellular pathologies and our study provides an important foundation upon which future investigations of DDX3X mutations may be compared.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different mutation types have different effects.

claim: RCOR2 binds to Insulinoma-associated 1, a transcription factor required in IPs for neurogenesis.
source: Indeed, RCOR2 binds to Insulinoma-associated 1 (Monaghan et al., 2017), a transcription factor required in IPs for neurogenesis (Farkas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing RCOR2 and Insm1 function.

claim: Many epigenetic regulators and chromatin-modifying enzymes are implicated in ID and ASD.
source: DDX3X-mediated epigenetic regulation will be fascinating to investigate in future studies, especially considering that many epigenetic regulators and chromatin-modifying enzymes are implicated in ID and ASD (Grafodatskaya et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article on epigenetics in neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: Reduced TE of DDX3X-dependent transcripts collectively contributes to phenotypes in mouse models and perhaps in human DDX3X syndrome.
source: We speculate that reduced TE of DDX3X-dependent transcripts collectively contributes to phenotypes in mouse models and perhaps in human DDX3X syndrome.
evidence: Speculated based on the identification of multiple DDX3X-dependent targets with roles in neurogenesis.

claim: Increasing TE of any one transcript would not alleviate Ddx3x LoF phenotypes.
source: Given that Ddx3x LoF modestly affects TE of many transcripts in neural progenitors, we do not anticipate that increasing TE of any one transcript would alleviate Ddx3x LoF phenotypes.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that multiple targets are affected.

claim: Widespread apoptosis is likely a substantial contributor to the reduced cortical area in cKO female mice.
source: Altogether, these data suggest widespread apoptosis is likely a substantial contributor to the reduced cortical area in cKO female mice.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between apoptosis and microcephaly in cKO females.

claim: Ddx3x depletion prolongs overall cell cycle in vivo, without a clear bias towards any specific phase.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that Ddx3x depletion prolongs overall cell cycle in vivo, without a clear bias towards any specific phase.
evidence: Inferred from cell cycle measurements showing increased Tc but no specific phase changes.

claim: Progenitors in vitro reflect in vivo phenotypes.
source: These data are consistent with the longer cell cycle measured in vivo, demonstrating that progenitors in vitro reflect in vivo phenotypes.
evidence: Inferred from consistency between in vivo and in vitro cell cycle measurements.

claim: Ddx3x is required across all stages of corticogenesis.
source: These data indicate that Ddx3x is essential for proper neuron number and suggests it is required across all stages of corticogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that multiple neuronal layers are affected.

claim: Observed differences in TE might reflect developmental stepwise translational repression.
source: Moreover, these results indicate that observed differences in TE might reflect developmental stepwise translational repression.
evidence: Inferred from the divergence in TE between early and late neuronal transcripts.

claim: uORFs frequently cause translational repression of the downstream, canonical ORF.
source: Ribo-seq can also reveal the use of upstream open reading frames (uORFs), which frequently cause translational repression of the downstream, canonical ORF (Johnstone et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of uORF function and supported by citation.

claim: The Ribo-seq dataset provides a valuable resource to interrogate the use of uORFs during cortical development.
source: Thus, this rich dataset provides a valuable resource to interrogate the use of uORFs during cortical development and suggests an important mode of gene expression regulation in the developing cortex.
evidence: Inferred from the identification of numerous uORFs in the dataset.

claim: About half of the TE changes in DDX3X targets were driven by changes in the input RNA levels while the other half had significantly lower TE with little to no change in the corresponding input RNA.
source: About half of these TE changes were driven by changes in the input RNA levels while the other half had significantly lower TE with little to no change in the corresponding input RNA.
evidence: Supported by analysis of Ribo-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The shift of DDX3X-dependent translation targets towards monosomes and concomitant depletion from polysomes was specific.
source: These shifts of DDX3X-dependent translation targets towards monosomes and concomitant depletion from polysomes were specific. For example, β-actin levels, were comparable between monosome fractions (β-actin CT average 25.06 vs 24.58) and polysome fractions (β-actin CT average 22.73 vs 22.72) of cHet females/cKO males and controls.
evidence: Supported by comparison with control transcript (β-actin) in polysome fractionation.

claim: The shift towards monosomes along with reduced TE reflects an essential requirement of DDX3X for translation of specific mRNAs in cortical progenitors in vivo.
source: Altogether the shift towards monosomes along with reduced TE reflects an essential requirement of DDX3X for translation of specific mRNAs in cortical progenitors in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from polysome fractionation and Ribo-seq data.

claim: Decreased TE of Setd3, as well as other DDX3X-dependent targets, may synergistically contribute to Ddx3x LoF neurogenesis phenotypes.
source: This suggests that decreased TE of Setd3, as well as other DDX3X-dependent targets, may synergistically contribute to Ddx3x LoF neurogenesis phenotypes (Figure 7F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Setd3 knockdown phenocopies Ddx3x loss and illustrated in Figure 7F.
